finding.claim: Delete authorization result is discarded, so any caller (including unauthenticated, g.user=None) can delete any stored file.
finding.source: Path parameter fid on DELETE /files/<fid> (views.py:15-16); no authentication required.
finding.sink: del STORE[fid] at views.py:19, after require_allowed() call at views.py:18 whose bool return is ignored.

trace.note: require_allowed (acl.is_allowed) is called; it returns a bool and never aborts, so the result is dropped.
is_allowed is a predicate returning bool, not a guard.
Object is deleted regardless of the check outcome.

finding.guards_checked: before_request load_user (views.py:10-12) only copies a header into g.user and enforces nothing; no auth decorator on the route; is_allowed is not ensure_allowed (which calls abort(403) at acl.py:10); rename route at views.py:26 uses ensure_allowed correctly, so the bug is specific to delete.

verdict.guard_found: None effective. The only candidate control is require_allowed (alias of acl.is_allowed, views.py:4, acl.py:4), which returns a bool. Its result is discarded as a bare statement at views.py:18, so nothing aborts before del STORE[fid] at views.py:19. ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10, abort(403)) is not called on this route. load_user (views.py:10-12) only copies a header into g.user and enforces nothing. No auth decorator is on the route at views.py:15.
verdict.reason: The DELETE handler at views.py:18 calls the bool-returning is_allowed (acl.py:4) and discards the result, so del STORE[fid] at views.py:19 runs for any caller, including anonymous requests where g.user is None (views.py:12); the rename route at views.py:26 uses ensure_allowed, which aborts at acl.py:10, so the bug is specific to delete.

finding.claim: g.user is taken from the client-supplied X-Session-User-Verified header without verification, allowing impersonation of any user who holds grants.
finding.source: HTTP request header X-Session-User-Verified, fully attacker-controlled.
finding.sink: Identity used for authorization: ensure_allowed(g.user, f, 'write') at views.py:26, which gates the rename write at views.py:27.

trace.note: g.user set from raw request header with no signature, session, or proxy check.
write grant checked against the spoofed g.user.
ensure_allowed aborts 403 only if is_allowed is false for that name.

finding.guards_checked: No header signature or server-side session validation in this code; anonymous (absent header -> None) is denied by grants.get(None, []), so exposure is limited to impersonating users who hold grants. Conditional on deployment: exploitable only if the service is reachable without a trusted upstream proxy that strips and sets this header.

verdict.guard_found: None in the code. views.py:12 copies the raw X-Session-User-Verified header into g.user with no signature, session, or proxy check. views.py:26 calls ensure_allowed, and acl.py:8-10 aborts with 403 only when is_allowed(user, ...) is False, so it is an effective gate, but it checks the spoofed identity. Anonymous requests (header absent, g.user None) are denied by grants.get(None, []) at acl.py:5. views.py:27 then applies the rename.
verdict.reason: views.py:12 trusts the client-supplied header as identity, and the only authorization check at views.py:26 (acl.py:8-10) runs against that value, so any client who can reach the service and knows a username holding a write grant can rename files as that user. Exploitability depends on deployment: if a trusted proxy strips and sets this header, the attacker cannot reach it, and that proxy is not in this code.
